data.title: Lactation duration and development of type 2 diabetes and metabolic syndrome in postpartum women with recent gestational diabetes mellitus.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
The World Health Organization and United Nations Children's Fund recommend exclusive breastfeeding (EBF) for the first six months of an infant's life. Although evidence suggests that maintaining breastfeeding has positive impacts on glucose and lipid metabolism in postpartum women with a history of gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), no study has investigated whether such effects differ between breastfeeding intensities. This study aimed to evaluate the impact of maintaining breastfeeding on prediabetes, type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), and metabolic syndrome (MetS) six months postpartum in women with GDM. This study also examined the potential variations in glucometabolic outcomes between EBF at six months and partial breastfeeding at six months.
METHODS
This prospective cohort study included 130 women with recent GDM who experienced live births between 7 September 2020 and 31 January 2023 at a university hospital in Bangkok, Thailand. All the women were free of T2DM and MetS at baseline (six weeks postpartum). We followed up these women six months postpartum to assess their breastfeeding practices (EBF at six months, partial breastfeeding at six months, or not maintaining breastfeeding) and evaluate their progression to prediabetes, T2DM, and MetS. Maintaining breastfeeding was defined as breastfeeding for six months. EBF was determined using the "recall since birth" method.
RESULTS
Of the 130 participants included, the rates of prediabetes, T2DM, and MetS six months postpartum were 33% (n = 43), 2% (n = 3), and 17% (n = 22), respectively. In the unadjusted model, maintaining breastfeeding was associated with a reduction in the risks of prediabetes and MetS but not T2DM. After adjusting for potential confounders, maintaining breastfeeding was a significant protective factor only for prediabetes. The adjusted risk ratios and 95% confidence intervals were 0.54 (0.29, 0.99) for prediabetes and 0.47 (0.19, 1.06) for MetS. When EBF at six months and partial breastfeeding at six months were separately analyzed, the risks of prediabetes and MetS differed between the two groups. In the EBF at six months-to-partial breastfeeding at six months comparison, the adjusted risk ratios (95% confidence intervals) of prediabetes and MetS were 0.46 (0.22, 0.97) vs. 0.79 (0.25, 2.49) and 0.34 (0.11, 0.99) vs. 0.69 (0.22, 2.07), respectively.
CONCLUSIONS
Maintaining breastfeeding reduced the risk of prediabetes and MetS, but not of T2DM, six months postpartum; these effects were significant only with EBF. These findings indicate that supporting maternal efforts to practice EBF for six months may improve women's health after GDM.
TRIAL REGISTRATION
Thai Clinical Trials Registry Registration No. TCTR20200902003. Date of registration: September 2, 2020. Date of initial participant enrollment: September 7, 2020.

data.title: Contraception and the risk of type 2 diabetes mellitus in Latina women with prior gestational diabetes mellitus.
data.abstract:
CONTEXT
Effective contraception is essential in women with prior gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) but should not increase their already substantial risk of developing type 2 diabetes.
OBJECTIVE
To determine whether exposure to low-dose oral contraceptives increases the risk of developing type 2 diabetes mellitus in women with recent GDM.
DESIGN
Retrospective cohort study of 904 Latinas with GDM who gave birth between January 1987 and March 1994, in whom postpartum diabetes was excluded at 4 to 16 weeks post partum.
INTERVENTIONS
At their initial postpartum visit, 443 women selected a nonhormonal form of contraception, 383 received a low-dose, estrogen-progestin combination oral contraceptive (OC), and 78 breast-feeding women received the progestin-only OC. When breast-feeding ended, patients initially taking progestin-only OCs were switched to combination OCs. Patients were followed up periodically with oral glucose tolerance tests for up to 7 1/2 years.
MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES
Person time was used to compute unadjusted average annual incidence rates of developing diabetes mellitus, as defined by the National Diabetes Data Group Criteria. Survival analysis was used to compute the unadjusted cumulative incidence rates and adjusted relative risks of diabetes mellitus.
RESULTS
The unadjusted average annual incidence rates of type 2 diabetes mellitus were 8.7%, 10.4%, and 26.5%, respectively, for patients using nonhormonal forms of contraception, combination OCs, and progestin-only OCs. Cumulative incidence rates were virtually identical for patients with uninterrupted use of combination OCs and nonhormonal forms of contraception, but patients using progestin-only OCs developed diabetes mellitus more rapidly during the first 2 years of use. After adjustment for potential confounding factors, the use of progestin-only OCs almost tripled the risk of type 2 diabetes mellitus compared with equivalent use of low-dose combination OCs (adjusted relative risk, 2.87; 95% confidence interval, 1.57-5.27). The magnitude of this risk increased with duration of uninterrupted use.
CONCLUSION
Progestin-only OCs were associated with an increased risk of diabetes in breast-feeding Latinas with recent GDM and probably should be prescribed with caution, if at all, in these women. Long-term use of low-dose combination OCs did not increase the risk of type 2 diabetes compared with use of nonhormonal contraception. Thus, combination OCs do not appear to increase the risk of diabetes in non-breast-feeding women with recent GDM.

data.title: Breastfeeding Duration and Development of Dysglycemia in Women Who Had Gestational Diabetes Mellitus: Evidence from the GUSTO Cohort Study.
data.abstract: (1) Background: Breastfeeding has been shown to support glucose homeostasis in women after a pregnancy complicated by gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) and is potentially effective at reducing long-term diabetes risk. (2) Methods: Data from the Growing Up in Singapore Towards healthy Outcomes (GUSTO) study were analyzed to understand the influence of breastfeeding duration on long-term dysglycemia (prediabetes and diabetes) risk in women who had GDM in the index pregnancy. GDM and dysglycemia four to seven years postpartum were determined by the oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT). A Poisson regression model with a robust error variance was used to estimate incidence rate ratios (IRRs) for dysglycemia four to seven years post-delivery according to groupings of the duration of any breastfeeding (<1, ≥1 to <6, and ≥6 months). (3) Results: Women who had GDM during the index pregnancy and complete breastfeeding information and OGTT four to seven years postpartum were included in this study ( n = 116). Fifty-one women (44%) had postpartum dysglycemia. Unadjusted IRRs showed an inverse association between dysglycemia risk and ≥1 month to <6 months (IRR 0.91; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.57, 1.43; p = 0.68) and ≥6 months (IRR 0.50; 95% CI 0.27, 0.91; p = 0.02) breastfeeding compared to <1 month of any breastfeeding. After adjusting for key confounders, the IRR for the ≥6 months group remained significant (IRR 0.42; 95% CI 0.22, 0.80; p = 0.008). (4) Conclusions: Our results suggest that any breastfeeding of six months or longer may reduce long-term dysglycemia risk in women with a history of GDM in an Asian setting. Breastfeeding has benefits for mothers beyond weight loss, particularly for those with GDM.

data.title: Intensive lactation among women with recent gestational diabetes significantly alters the early postpartum circulating lipid profile: the SWIFT study.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Women with a history of gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) have a 7-fold higher risk of developing type 2 diabetes (T2D). It is estimated that 20-50% of women with GDM history will progress to T2D within 10 years after delivery. Intensive lactation could be negatively associated with this risk, but the mechanisms behind a protective effect remain unknown.
METHODS
In this study, we utilized a prospective GDM cohort of 1010 women without T2D at 6-9 weeks postpartum (study baseline) and tested for T2D onset up to 8 years post-baseline (n=980). Targeted metabolic profiling was performed on fasting plasma samples collected at both baseline and follow-up (1-2 years post-baseline) during research exams in a subset of 350 women (216 intensive breastfeeding, IBF vs. 134 intensive formula feeding or mixed feeding, IFF/Mixed). The relationship between lactation intensity and circulating metabolites at both baseline and follow-up were evaluated to discover underlying metabolic responses of lactation and to explore the link between these metabolites and T2D risk.
RESULTS
We observed that lactation intensity was strongly associated with decreased glycerolipids (TAGs/DAGs) and increased phospholipids/sphingolipids at baseline. This lipid profile suggested decreased lipogenesis caused by a shift away from the glycerolipid metabolism pathway towards the phospholipid/sphingolipid metabolism pathway as a component of the mechanism underlying the benefits of lactation. Longitudinal analysis demonstrated that this favorable lipid profile was transient and diminished at 1-2 years postpartum, coinciding with the cessation of lactation. Importantly, when stratifying these 350 women by future T2D status during the follow-up (171 future T2D vs. 179 no T2D), we discovered that lactation induced robust lipid changes only in women who did not develop incident T2D. Subsequently, we identified a cluster of metabolites that strongly associated with future T2D risk from which we developed a predictive metabolic signature with a discriminating power (AUC) of 0.78, superior to common clinical variables (i.e., fasting glucose, AUC 0.56 or 2-h glucose, AUC 0.62).
CONCLUSIONS
In this study, we show that intensive lactation significantly alters the circulating lipid profile at early postpartum and that women who do not respond metabolically to lactation are more likely to develop T2D. We also discovered a 10-analyte metabolic signature capable of predicting future onset of T2D in IBF women. Our findings provide novel insight into how lactation affects maternal metabolism and its link to future diabetes onset.
TRIAL REGISTRATION
ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01967030 .

trajectory.final_answer:
# Key Findings

## Incidence of Type 2 Diabetes (T2D) after Gestational Diabetes (GDM)
- Women with a history of GDM have a substantially higher risk of progressing to T2D than women with normoglycemic pregnancies. A large systematic review and meta-analysis reported an overall relative risk of 9.51 (95% CI 7.14–12.67) for T2D after GDM versus controls, with a pooled cumulative incidence of approximately 16.5% in mixed populations over extended follow-up, and lower estimates in predominantly White cohorts, though subgroup differences were not statistically significant across populations<cite id="32404325">Women with a history of GDM have a nearly 10-fold higher risk of developing T2DM than healthy controls, with a pooled relative risk of 9.51 (95% CI 7.14 to 12.67); cumulative incidence was 16.46% in mixed ethnicity, 15.58% in predominantly non-white, and 9.91% in white populations, with no significant differences between subgroups</cite>. 
- Another meta-analysis of 28 cohorts (170,139 women) estimated a pooled incidence rate of T2D after GDM of 26.20 per 1000 person-years (95% CI 23.31–29.10), with risk increasing linearly over time (e.g., 19.7% at 10 years, 29.4% at 20 years, and 58.3% at 50 years). Higher risk was observed in Asian regions, older age, and higher BMI, and the lowest incidence was noted when GDM was diagnosed using IADPSG criteria<cite id="32405502">The pooled incidence of T2DM after GDM was 26.20 per 1000 person-years; risk increased with duration of follow-up and was higher in Asia, older age, and higher BMI, with the lowest incidence under IADPSG-diagnosed GDM</cite>. 
- A separate systematic review and meta-analysis (39 cohorts, 2,847,596 women) found a pooled unadjusted risk of T2D after GDM of 8.92 (95% CI 7.84–10.14), with higher risk among older women, those with a family history of diabetes, and certain racial/ethnic groups and regions<cite id="34782531">A pooled unadjusted RR of 8.92 (95% CI 7.84–10.14) for T2DM after GDM was observed, with higher risk in older women, those with a family history of diabetes, Black and non-Hispanic White women, and in Europe and South-East Asia</cite>. 
- Beyond T2D, women with GDM also face increased cardiovascular risk even without progressing to T2D, with a twofold higher risk of future cardiovascular events and a 56% higher risk when analyses were restricted to women without incident T2D, with elevated risk apparent within the first decade postpartum<cite id="30843102">Women with GDM had a twofold higher risk of future cardiovascular events (RR 1.98) and a 56% higher risk (RR 1.56) when restricted to those without T2D, with increased risk in the first decade postpartum</cite>. 

## Postpartum Factors That Strongly Predict Progression

- BMI: Higher pre-pregnancy BMI (≥25 kg/m²) is associated with increased risk of T2D after GDM in cohort analyses, with multivariate models indicating that elevated BMI contributes independently to progression risk<cite id="26385131">An increased risk of developing type 2 diabetes after GDM was observed among women with early pregnancy BMI ≥25 kg/m²</cite>. A meta-analysis further shows that higher BMI categories are linked to higher long-term T2D risk post-GDM, consistent with the broader literature on adiposity and diabetes risk<cite id="32405502">Higher BMI was associated with increased risk of T2DM after GDM in pooled analyses</cite>. 
- Breastfeeding: Evidence suggests that longer duration of any breastfeeding is associated with lower risk of postpartum dysglycemia (prediabetes and diabetes) in women with prior GDM. In the GUSTO cohort, ≥6 months of any breastfeeding was associated with a significantly lower risk of dysglycemia (adjusted IRR 0.42, 95% CI 0.22–0.80) compared with <1 month, while effects were attenuated but still suggestive for 1–5 months of breastfeeding<cite id="33525398">≥6 months of any breastfeeding was associated with a lower long-term dysglycemia risk (adjusted IRR 0.42, 95% CI 0.22–0.80) versus <1 month in women with prior GDM</cite>. A prospective cohort (SWIFT) found that intensive breastfeeding altered circulating lipid profiles in ways consistent with improved metabolic health, and that women who did not respond metabolically to lactation were more likely to develop T2D during follow-up, suggesting lactation responsiveness as a predictive biomarker<cite id="34620173">Intensive lactation altered postpartum lipid profiles, and women who did not respond metabolically were more likely to develop T2D; a 10-analyte metabolic signature predicted future T2D with AUC 0.78</cite>. A Thai cohort reported that maintaining breastfeeding reduced risks of prediabetes and metabolic syndrome at 6 months postpartum, with exclusive breastfeeding at 6 months showing stronger associations than partial breastfeeding, though T2D reduction was not significant after adjustment<cite id="38610024">Maintaining breastfeeding (exclusive at 6 months preferred) reduced prediabetes and metabolic syndrome at 6 months postpartum, but T2DM reduction was not significant after adjustment</cite>. Observational data from Australia also identified only breastfeeding at discharge as a contributor to increased T2D risk when other factors were controlled, highlighting the complex interplay of lactation patterns and metabolic trajectory<cite id="26385131">Only breastfeeding at hospital discharge contributed to increased T2D risk in multivariate analysis, alongside higher BMI and early GDM diagnosis</cite>. 
- Postpartum Glucose Levels and Testing: While specific postpartum OGTT 2-hour glucose thresholds predicting progression were not retrieved in the immediate search, cohort studies emphasize the importance of postpartum glucose testing for early risk stratification. Women with GDM are often identified as an at-risk group for incident T2D, and postpartum screening is recommended to detect dysglycemia and initiate preventive measures. In the absence of T2D diagnosis, elevated cardiovascular risk persists, underscoring the value of ongoing metabolic surveillance beyond immediate postpartum testing<cite id="30843102">Women with GDM comprise an at-risk population for cardiovascular events even without progressing to T2D, supporting early risk factor surveillance and modification</cite>. 
- Other Modifiable Risk Factors: Contraception choice may influence risk; in Latinas with prior GDM followed for up to 7.5 years, progestin-only oral contraceptives were associated with an increased risk of T2D compared with low-dose combination pills (adjusted RR 2.87, 95% CI 1.57–5.27), particularly in the first 2 years of use, whereas nonhormonal contraception had similar cumulative incidence to combination pills over time<cite id="9707143">Progestin-only OCs almost tripled the risk of T2D compared with low-dose combination OCs (adjusted RR 2.87, 95% CI 1.57–5.27), especially within the first 2 years, while nonhormonal and combination OCs had similar cumulative incidence</cite>. 
- Early Life Course Factors: Age at GDM diagnosis and ethnicity also contribute. Early GDM diagnosis (e.g., prior to 17 weeks) and older maternal age were associated with higher postpartum T2D risk in multivariable models, and Indigenous populations in Australia showed greater than fourfold higher hazards of T2D after GDM compared with non-Indigenous women, with substantial cumulative incidence by 8 years<cite id="26385131">Early GDM diagnosis (prior to 17 weeks) and higher BMI were associated with increased risk; Indigenous women had >4-fold higher risk and 21.9–42.4% cumulative incidence by 3–7 years postpartum</cite>. 

## Implications for Clinical Practice
- Intensive lifestyle interventions initiated postpartum can reduce modifiable risk factors: a meta-analysis of RCTs showed postpartum diet/physical activity interventions reduced diabetes risk by about 11% and improved weight, BMI, and waist circumference, though glycemic markers showed less consistent change, suggesting that anthropometric improvements may be early indicators of reduced diabetes risk<cite id="38727771">Postpartum lifestyle interventions reduced diabetes risk by 11% and improved weight, BMI, and waist circumference, though fasting glucose, 2-h glucose, and HbA1c changes were not significant</cite>. 
- Given the strong and sustained risk of T2D after GDM and the early emergence of cardiovascular risk, comprehensive postpartum care should include structured glucose testing, counseling on weight management, promotion of exclusive and sustained breastfeeding, and consideration of contraceptive choices that minimize metabolic risk<cite id="30843102">Postpartum cardiovascular risk is elevated even without T2D, supporting early surveillance and risk modification</cite><cite id="9707143">Progestin-only contraceptives increase T2D risk in women with prior GDM, whereas low-dose combination pills do not increase risk compared with nonhormonal methods</cite>. 

## Summary
- The incidence of T2D after GDM is high, with pooled incidence around 8–10 fold higher than in women without GDM and approximately 26 per 1000 person-years in meta-analyses, rising over time and influenced by higher BMI, older age, Asian region, and IADPSG-defined GDM<cite id="32404325">Women with prior GDM have nearly 10-fold higher T2D risk, with cumulative incidence around 16% in mixed populations</cite><cite id="32405502">Pooled incidence is 26.2 per 1000 person-years, increasing with follow-up and higher with BMI and older age</cite><cite id="34782531">Pooled unadjusted RR 8.92, with higher risk in older and family history-positive women and certain regions</cite>. 
- Among postpartum factors, higher BMI and longer breastfeeding duration show the strongest and most consistent associations with lower dysglycemia/T2D risk, while early GDM diagnosis, older age, and ethnicity (e.g., Indigenous status) are robust predictors of higher risk; postpartum glucose testing and lifestyle interventions are key for risk reduction and early detection<cite id="26385131">Higher BMI and early GDM diagnosis (before 17 weeks) predict higher risk; Indigenous status predicts >4-fold higher hazards</cite><cite id="33525398">≥6 months of any breastfeeding is associated with significantly lower dysglycemia risk</cite><cite id="38610024">Maintaining breastfeeding reduces prediabetes and metabolic syndrome at 6 months</cite><cite id="34620173">Metabolic response to lactation may predict future T2D risk</cite>.

Authors: Wattacheril, Julia J, Abdelmalek, Manal F, Lim, Joseph K et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: Gastroenterology
Abstract: DESCRIPTION
The purpose of this American Gastroenterological Association (AGA) Clinical Practice Update Expert Review is to provide clinicians with guidance on the use of noninvasive tests (NITs) in the evaluation and management of patients with nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). NAFLD affects nearly 30% of the global population and is a growing cause of end-stage liver disease and liver-related health care resource utilization. However, only a minority of all patients with NAFLD experience a liver-related outcome. It is therefore critically important for clinicians to assess prognosis and identify those with increased risk of disease progression and negative clinical outcomes at the time of initial assessment. We performed sex-specific, age-adjusted Pearson correlation coefficients, as well as multivariable-adjusted linear and logistic regression models.

In our study sample (n = 2201, 54.1% women, average age 54 years old, average BMI 27.1 kg/m 2 ) the prevalence of fibrosis was 7.7%. Abstract: BACKGROUND
Given the worldwide prevalence of NAFLD and NASH, there is a need to develop treatments to slow or reverse disease progression. Thirty subjects (13 females, 46-71 years) with NASH and advanced fibrosis were recruited. Subjects were randomized to receive 8 mg.kg-1 GR-MD-02 (via IV infusion) or placebo, administered biweekly over a 16-week period. Therapeutic efficacy was examined using cT1, MRE, and LSM. Statistical analyses on group differences in the biomarkers were performed using robust ANCOVA models adjusting for baseline measurement and additional covariates.

There was also no significant difference in liver stiffness, measured by MRE (p = 0.80) or LSM (p = 0.63), between groups. Examination of repeatability of the cT1, MRE and LSM revealed coefficient of variations of 3.1%, 11% and 40% respectively.

8 mg.kg-1 of GR-MD-02 had no significant effect on non-invasive biomarkers of liver inflammation or fibrosis over a 4-month period. Histological confirmation was not available in this study. # Summary

- Longitudinal cohort data show that increases in liver stiffness by magnetic resonance elastography (MRE) predict histologic fibrosis progression, including progression from early to advanced fibrosis, supporting MRE as a prognostic marker in NAFLD/NASH. <cite id="31556124">A 15% increase in MRE stiffness was associated with increased odds of fibrosis progression (OR 3.56 unadjusted; OR 3.36 adjusted), and specifically predicted progression to advanced fibrosis (OR 4.90)</cite>.

- Among noninvasive markers, composite indices such as FIB-4 and other panels (e.g., BARD for NASH) are widely used; guidelines emphasize combining modalities when needed and repeating tests longitudinally to capture progression. <cite id="37542503">A Fibrosis 4 Index score <1.3 is associated with strong negative predictive value for advanced fibrosis; a combination of two or more NITs is preferred for patients with FIB-4 >1.3; serial monitoring using LSM, VCTE, or MRE is recommended</cite>.

# Imaging-based scores and their prognostic value

- MRE: Demonstrated prognostic value for fibrosis progression in NAFLD, with a 15% increase in stiffness predicting progression and particularly advancement to advanced fibrosis in a prospective cohort with paired MRE and biopsies. <cite id="31556124">A 15% increase in MRE predicted histologic fibrosis progression and progression to advanced fibrosis with clinically significant odds ratios</cite>.

- VCTE (FibroScan): Consensus and reviews recommend VCTE as part of longitudinal monitoring due to its correlation with portal pressure and clinical decompensation; serial measurements are advised in patients at risk (F3–F4). <cite id="37542503">Serial liver stiffness measurement or vibration-controlled transient elastography is recommended for monitoring progression in patients with NITs suggestive of F3–F4, given correlation with clinically significant portal hypertension and decompensation</cite>. <cite id="32118201">VCTE is a physical NIT but has limitations in capturing dynamic disease, supporting serial testing</cite>.

- MRI-based cT1 mapping: Useful for assessing fibro-inflammation; while promising, variability across modalities exists, and some biomarkers may have lower repeatability than others. <cite id="30192782">cT1 showed potential utility but with lower repeatability compared to MRE in a NASH trial, highlighting the need for robust, reproducible markers for longitudinal change</cite>.

# Practical recommendations for adults with NASH

- Initial risk stratification: Use FIB-4 to exclude advanced fibrosis (<1.3), then combine serum and imaging NITs when indeterminate or when risk needs refinement. <cite id="37542503">FIB-4 <1.3 has strong negative predictive value; combining two or more NITs is preferred when FIB-4 >1.3</cite>.

It is equally important to assess disease trajectory over time, particularly in response to currently available therapeutic approaches. There are, however, many limitations of liver biopsies and their reading that have limited their use in routine practice. The utilization of NITs facilitates risk stratification of patients and longitudinal assessment of disease progression for patients with NAFLD. These best practice advice statements were drawn from a review of the published literature and from expert opinion. BEST PRACTICE ADVICE 4: Use of NITs in accordance with manufacturer's specifications (eg, not in patients with ascites or pacemakers) can minimize risk of discordant results and adverse events. BEST PRACTICE ADVICE 5: NITs should be interpreted with context and consideration of pertinent clinical data (eg, physical examination, biochemical, radiographic, and endoscopic) to optimize positive predictive value in the identification of patients with advanced fibrosis. - VCTE (FibroScan): Consensus and reviews recommend VCTE as part of longitudinal monitoring due to its correlation with portal pressure and clinical decompensation; serial measurements are advised in patients at risk (F3–F4). <cite id="37542503">Serial liver stiffness measurement or vibration-controlled transient elastography is recommended for monitoring progression in patients with NITs suggestive of F3–F4, given correlation with clinically significant portal hypertension and decompensation</cite>. <cite id="32118201">VCTE is a physical NIT but has limitations in capturing dynamic disease, supporting serial testing</cite>.

- MRI-based cT1 mapping: Useful for assessing fibro-inflammation; while promising, variability across modalities exists, and some biomarkers may have lower repeatability than others. <cite id="30192782">cT1 showed potential utility but with lower repeatability compared to MRE in a NASH trial, highlighting the need for robust, reproducible markers for longitudinal change</cite>.

# Practical recommendations for adults with NASH

- Initial risk stratification: Use FIB-4 to exclude advanced fibrosis (<1.3), then combine serum and imaging NITs when indeterminate or when risk needs refinement. <cite id="37542503">FIB-4 <1.3 has strong negative predictive value; combining two or more NITs is preferred when FIB-4 >1.3</cite>.

- Monitoring progression: Repeat imaging-based stiffness tests (VCTE/MRE) and, where available, MRI-PDFF or cT1 to track progression, especially in patients with F3–F4 or high-risk features. <cite id="37542503">Serial LSM, VCTE, or MRE monitoring is advised for patients with advanced fibrosis/cirrhosis by NITs</cite>. <cite id="32118201">Given limitations of cross-sectional NITs, serial testing is more informative for longitudinal change</cite>.

- Prognostic thresholds: A 15% increase in MRE stiffness over time signals higher risk of fibrosis progression and may guide intensification of lifestyle or pharmacologic therapy. <cite id="31556124">A 15% increase in MRE stiffness confers significantly higher odds of fibrosis progression and advanced fibrosis development</cite>.

- Integration with clinical context: Use NITs alongside clinical, biochemical, radiologic, and endoscopic data; consider biopsy if results are discordant or indeterminate, particularly when outcomes are at stake. <cite id="37542503">NITs should be interpreted with clinical context; biopsy is recommended for indeterminate or discordant results or conflicting findings</cite>.

# Caveats and gaps

- While MRE and VCTE show prognostic value, variability and limitations of current NITs mean they should complement, not replace, clinical judgment and, when possible, confirmatory biopsy. <cite id="32118201">NITs have variability and accuracy limitations and were not designed to capture dynamic disease or longitudinal changes, so they should be complementary to biopsy</cite>.

- Some MRI-based markers (e.g., cT1) may have lower repeatability than MRE, and not all centers have access to MRI-PDFF or advanced elastography; test availability and operator dependence affect implementation. <cite id="30192782">cT1 showed lower repeatability than MRE, underscoring the importance of test selection and standardization</cite>.

# Bottom line

- For adults with NASH, the best prognostic noninvasive tools for progression to advanced fibrosis/cirrhosis over time are serial imaging-based liver stiffness measures—particularly VCTE/FibroScan and MRE—used in combination with serum fibrosis indices when needed, interpreted within clinical context, and repeated at intervals appropriate to risk and treatment. <cite id="37542503">Serial LSM, VCTE, or MRE monitoring is recommended for longitudinal assessment and management in NAFLD/NASH, especially for F3–F4</cite> <cite id="31556124">Increases in MRE stiffness predict histologic progression and advanced fibrosis</cite> <cite id="32118201">Current NITs have limitations and should be used serially and contextually</cite>.

<answer>
# Executive Summary

- Evidence that neuroinflammation drives disease in ALS and Huntington's disease (HD) converges on glial activation, complement-mediated synapse/motor neuron loss, and cytokine/chemokine signatures linked to clinical severity. In ALS, postmortem human studies show complement C1q and C3 deposition around motor neurons and TDP-43–positive neurons, microglial and astrocytic activation, and CSF/serum inflammatory markers correlating with progression; in HD, microglial activation and complement/surface molecule upregulation accompany striatal neuron loss and clinical decline. Consistently implicated pathways include complement cascades (C1q/C3), interferon/chemokine signaling (e.g., CXCL10/CX3CR1), and astrocyte/microglia reactivity; targeting these pathways in animal models can slow phenotypes, supporting causality.

# ALS: Evidence That Neuroinflammation Drives Disease and Pathways Linked to Severity

- Glial reactivity and complement tagging of dying neurons are central. In human ALS spinal cord, C1q and C3 are deposited on TDP-43–positive neurons and their processes, marking them for phagocytosis by microglia and contributing to motor neuron loss; this complement "eat-me" signaling is a hallmark of neurodegeneration and is specifically enriched in ALS tissue, implicating complement activation as a driver of disease progression rather than a mere consequence. Microglia and astrocytes show robust activation phenotypes around degenerating motor neurons, with dystrophic processes and pro-inflammatory gene programs, indicating functional neuroinflammation in human disease tissue.

- Inflammatory signatures in biofluids and imaging correlate with severity. Cytokine/chemokine profiles in ALS CSF and serum (e.g., interferon-γ, TNF-α, IL-6, and CXCL10) are elevated in progressive versus stable patients and associate with functional decline and survival; longitudinal neuroimaging shows that regions with higher microglial activation and gliosis have faster atrophy and motor unit loss, linking neuroinflammatory activity to clinical progression. These correlations strengthen the argument that active neuroinflammation, not just cell loss, drives worsening disease.

- Immune pathways most consistently associated with severity include:
  - Complement pathway (C1q, C3) — upregulated in ALS spinal cord and associated with neuronal targeting and microglial engulfment; higher expression correlates with greater motor neuron loss and faster disease progression in cohort data.
  - Interferon/chemokine signaling (e.g., CXCL10, IFN-γ response genes) — increased in blood and CSF of progressive ALS and linked to worse outcomes; interferon-stimulated genes in astrocytes and microglia associate with neuronal injury and disease speed.
  - Microglial activation state and migration toward degenerating axons/motor neurons — imaging and postmortem morphology show microglia adopt disease-associated phenotypes and physically interact with dying neurons; markers like CX3CR1 and MHC-II enrichment correlate with severity.
  - Astrocyte reactivity and scar formation — reactive astrocytes express S100β and other gliosis markers in ALS lesions and correlate with tissue damage and clinical decline.

- Causality and therapeutic angles. Mouse models of ALS demonstrate that blocking complement or modulating microglial reactivity can reduce motor neuron loss and extend survival, and that complement tagging (C1q/C3 deposition) on motor neurons accelerates microglial engulfment and disease. Conversely, pro-inflammatory priming worsens outcomes, while anti-inflammatory or complement-inhibitory interventions slow disease, supporting a mechanistic role for neuroinflammation in ALS progression.

# Huntington's Disease: Evidence That Neuroinflammation Drives Disease and Pathways Linked to Severity

- Microglial complement/surface molecule programs and neuronal loss. In human HD striatum, microglia exhibit disease-associated phenotypes with upregulation of complement components (e.g., C1q, C3), Fc receptors, and fractalkine (CX3CL1) signaling, surrounding and phagocytosing dystrophic axons and neurons; these changes precede overt loss in some contexts and correlate with synaptic pruning and neuronal dysfunction. Astrocyte reactivity with gliosis and cytokine production is also prominent, linking glial activation to striatal degeneration.

- Immune signatures track clinical severity. CSF and postmortem transcriptomic analyses in HD show elevated inflammatory cytokines/chemokines (e.g., IL-6, TNF-α, CXCL10) and increased microglial/astrocytic markers that correlate with disease stage and functional decline; imaging studies report that regions with higher microglial activation and complement expression show faster atrophy and worse cognitive/motor outcomes, paralleling ALS findings.

- Pathways most consistently associated with severity include:
  - Complement cascade (C1q, C3, CR3/CR4) — upregulated in HD striatum and associated with synapse elimination and neuronal loss; higher complement expression correlates with greater striatal atrophy and clinical severity.
  - Interferon/chemokine signaling (CXCL10, IFN-γ/ISGs) — increased in HD brain and CSF and linked to neuronal injury and disease progression; interferon-driven microglial activation and astrocyte reactivity associate with worse outcomes.
  - Microglial activation and CX3CR1/fractalkine axis — microglial morphological and molecular activation, plus fractalkine receptor signaling, correlate with disease spread and severity; targeting microglial reactivity can mitigate neurotoxic pruning in models.
  - Astrocyte reactivity and S100β/C3aR signaling — reactive astrocytes contribute to chronic inflammation and complement-mediated neurotoxicity, aligning with clinical decline.

- Causality in models. In HD mouse models, genetic or pharmacologic suppression of complement components or modulation of microglial reactivity reduces microglial engulfment of neurons/axons, preserves striatal circuit function, and slows behavioral decline, indicating that neuroinflammatory pathways actively drive disease progression and that their inhibition can be beneficial.

# Cross-Disease Convergence and Clinical Implications

- Convergent mechanisms: Both ALS and HD show complement-mediated "find/eat" signaling around dying neurons, microglial and astrocytic reactivity, and interferon/chemokine signatures that track with disease severity. These shared pathways suggest common therapeutic opportunities targeting complement, microglial activation, and astrocyte reactivity.

- Most consistently associated pathways with clinical severity across both diseases:
  - Complement pathway (C1q/C3) — robustly implicated in tagging and promoting phagocytosis of degenerating neurons and correlates with disease speed.
  - Interferon/chemokine signaling (CXCL10, IFN-γ/ISGs) — elevated and linked to worse outcomes in both ALS and HD cohorts.
  - Microglial activation and CX3CR1/fractalkine axis — activation state and motility correlate with neuronal injury and clinical decline.
  - Astrocyte reactivity/gliosis — markers of astrocyte activation associate with tissue damage and severity.

- Therapeutic evidence: In both diseases, anti-complement or microglia-modulating strategies in animal models slow phenotypes, while human biomarkers of ongoing neuroinflammation (e.g., CSF cytokines, complement levels, imaging-based glial activation) predict progression. This supports neuroinflammation as a driver and motivates clinical trials of complement inhibitors, microglial modulators, and interferon pathway blockers.

# Key Evidence Gaps

- Direct causal links in humans remain limited by access to longitudinal human tissue and biofluids; however, convergent human postmortem, imaging, and CSF/serum cohort data with model-based causality tests provide strong support. Future work should include prospective CSF/blood biomarker studies with spatial imaging of glial/complement activity and interventional trials targeting complement or microglial pathways to confirm clinical impact.

<snippet id="34546767">Title: Clinical Outcomes and Adverse Events after First-Line Treatment in Metastatic Renal Cell Carcinoma: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis.
Authors: Nocera, Luigi, Karakiewicz, Pierre I, Wenzel, Mike et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: The Journal of urology
Abstract: PURPOSE
Four recent first-line clinical trials leveraging immune-oncology agents demonstrated an overall survival (OS) benefit relative to sunitinib. We aimed to provide formal comparisons among immune-oncology combinations in terms of OS, progression-free survival (PFS), objective response rates and treatment-related adverse events (AEs).
MATERIALS AND METHODS
PubMed® database was searched for studies indexed from January 1, 2016 through March 6, 2021. Only phase III randomized clinical trials with proven OS benefit relative to sunitinib were included: CheckMate 214 (nivolumab plus ipilimumab [N+I]), KEYNOTE-426 (pembrolizumab plus axitinib [P+A]), CheckMate 9ER (nivolumab plus cabozantinib [N+C]) and KEYNOTE-581 (lenvatinib plus permbrolizumab [L+P]). OS represented the primary outcome. PFS, objective response rate and AEs represented secondary outcomes.
RESULTS
Overall, 3,320 patients were included. Regarding OS, N+C ranked first, followed by L+P, P+A and N+I. Regarding PFS and objective response rate, L+P ranked first, followed by N+C, P+A and N+I. Finally, N+I ranked first with respect to lowest grade 3+ AEs, followed by P+A, N+C and L+P. Differences in followup duration, risk grouping and nephrectomy rates distinguish the studies.
CONCLUSIONS
N+C may provide the most favorable OS, L+P the most favorable PFS and ORRs, and N+I the lowest toxicity. Population differences may potentially undermine the generalizability and the robustness of findings of metastatic renal cell carcinoma.</snippet>

<snippet id="39941888">Title: Real-World Efficacy and Toxicity of Ipilimumab and Nivolumab as First-Line Treatment of Metastatic Renal Cell Carcinoma (mRCC) in a Subpopulation of Elderly and Poor Performance Status Patients.
Authors: Shani Shrem, Noa, Beltran-Bless, Ana-Alicia, Ghosh, Sunita et al. | Year: 2025 | Journal: Cancers
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Ipilimumab and nivolumab (ipi/nivo) improved overall survival (OS) compared to sunitinib in the pivotal Checkmate 214 trial of metastatic renal cell carcinoma (mRCC) with International Metastatic RCC Database Consortium (IMDC) intermediate/poor risk disease. We evaluated the efficacy and toxicity of ipi/nivo in older and frailer populations in a real-world mRCC cohort.
METHODS
Analysis was conducted on a real-world cohort with mRCC (N = 551) treated with first-line ipi/nivo from the Canadian Kidney Cancer information system (CKCis) database from January 2014 to December 2021. A comparison was made between outcomes and toxicity in patients 1. <70 versus (vs.) ≥70 yo, 2. <75 vs. ≥75 yo, and 3. KPS ≥70 vs. <70 yo. OS, progression-free survival (PFS), and time to treatment failure (TTF) were calculated by Kaplan-Meier analysis. Log-rank tests were used for comparison between groups.
RESULTS
Ipi/nivo treatment had no impact on survival outcomes or toxicity for patients >70 yo and >75 yo when controlled for IMDC. However, when comparing patients with KPS > 70 vs. KPS < 70, patients with a poor performance status had decreased median OS at 54.5 m vs. 10.8 m ( p -value < 0.0001) and PFS at 11.6 vs. 3.1 m ( p -value < 0.0001).
CONCLUSIONS
The use of ipi/nivo in mRCC demonstrated similar survival outcomes and toxicity in an older patient population. In patients with a poor performance status, it was associated with inferior OS and PFS. We believe that ipi/nivo is a reasonable treatment option for these patient populations, particularly in older patients.</snippet>
<snippet id="30616146">Title: Second-line targeted therapies after nivolumab-ipilimumab failure in metastatic renal cell carcinoma.
Authors: Auvray, Marie, Auclin, Edouard, Barthelemy, Philippe et al. | Year: 2019 | Journal: European journal of cancer (Oxford, England : 1990)
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Nivolumab-ipilimumab demonstrated a survival benefit over sunitinib in first-line setting for metastatic renal cell carcinomas (mRCCs) and is becoming a new standard of care for naïve patients with intermediate or poor risk prognosis (International mRCC Database Consortium). The efficacy of subsequent vascular endothelial growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) after nivolumab-ipilimumab failure remains unclear.
METHODS
Medical records of mRCC patients treated with nivolumab-ipilimumab, who received subsequent TKI, as part of Checkmate 214 study were reviewed in 13 institutions. Baseline characteristics, outcome data including progression-free survival (PFS), response, overall survival (OS) and toxicities were retrospectively collected.
RESULTS
Overall 33 patients received subsequent TKI after nivolumab-ipilimumab failure. Median follow-up from start of subsequent TKI is 22 months (19-NR). Best response was assessed in 30 patients: 12 partial responses (36%), 13 stable diseases (39%) and five progressive diseases (15%). Median PFS from start of TKI was 8 months [5-13]. Median PFS with first-generation (sunitinib/pazopanib) and second-generation TKI (axitinib/cabozantinib) was 8 months [5-16] and 7 months (5-NA), respectively. PFS in second line was significantly longer in patients with a long first-line duration of response to the double immune checkpoint blockade (≥6 months) with 8 versus 5 months for short responder (<6 months) (p = 0.03). OS rate was 54% at 12 months. Toxicity was as expected: 42% developed at least one toxicity grade ≥3.
CONCLUSION
This is the first report of outcomes with TKI, after first-line nivolumab-ipilimumab failure. Median PFS suggests a sustained benefit of TKI and supports trials investigating the optimal sequence.</snippet>
<snippet id="29587324">Title: [Immunotherapy for renal cell carcinoma - current status].
Authors: Grimm, Marc-Oliver, Foller, Susan | Year: 2018 | Journal: Aktuelle Urologie
Abstract: Systemic treatment of metastatic renal cell carcinoma (mRCC) has substantially changed during the last 2 years due to approval of the immune-checkpoint inhibitor Nivolumab (Opdivo ® ) and new multikinase inhibitors (Cabozantinib, Lenvatinib, Tivozanib). The german kidney tumor guideline strongly recommends Nivolumab and Cabozantinib as 2nd line treatments after prior VEGF targeted therapy. CheckMate 025, the prospective randomized trial which led to approval of Nivolumab demonstrated improved overall survival (26 month vs. 19.7 month; hazard ratio 0.73; p = 0.0006) and response rate (26 % vs. 5 %) as well as a favorable toxicity profile compared with Everolimus. Currently, numerous combinations with PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors are compared to Sunitinib as first line treatment of mRCC. Out of these CheckMate 214, a randomized phase-3 trial is the first to demonstrate a significant higher objective response rate (42 % vs. 27 %, p < 0.0001) and overall survival (Sunitinib 26.0 month, median for Nivo + Ipi has been not yet reached (28.2 - NR); Hazard ratio 0.63) for the combination of Nivolumab and the CTLA-4 antibody Ipilimumab in IMDC intermediate and high risk patients. Furthermore, CheckMate 214 shows better side effect profile and quality of life in patients receiving Nivolumab and Ipilimumab compared with Sunitinib. However, a considerable increase of immune related adverse events is associated with the immune combination therapy. Another randomized trial demonstrates improved progression-free survival for the combination of the PD-L1 inhibitor Atezolizumab and the VEGF antibody Bevacizumab in patients with PD-L1 positive tumors; this was found in all IMDC risk groups. <snippet id="32800717">Title: Clinical Activity of Ipilimumab Plus Nivolumab in Patients With Metastatic Non-Clear Cell Renal Cell Carcinoma.
Authors: Gupta, Ruby, Ornstein, Moshe Chaim, Li, Hong et al. | Year: 2020 | Journal: Clinical genitourinary cancer
Abstract: INTRODUCTION
Ipilimumab plus nivolumab has been approved for intermediate- and poor-risk metastatic renal cell carcinoma (RCC). However, the activity in non-clear cell RCC (nccRCC) is unknown.
PATIENTS AND METHODS
Patients from Cleveland Clinic and the University of Texas Southwestern who had received ipilimumab plus nivolumab for metastatic nccRCC from October 2017 to May 2019 were retrospectively identified. Ipilimumab plus nivolumab was administered in accordance with the CHECKMATE 214 trial. Imaging was obtained at baseline and every 12 weeks. The baseline patient characteristics, objective response per Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors, version 1.1, and treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) per Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events, version 5.0, were analyzed.
RESULTS
Eighteen patients were identified. The median age was 59 years (range, 32-81 years), 77.8% were men, and the Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status was 0 (38%) or 1 (50%). The median treatment duration was 2.4 months (range, 0.7-12.3 months). The non-clear cell histologic types included 6 papillary, 5 chromophobe, 3 unclassified, 2 adenocarcinoma of renal origin, 1 translocation, and 1 medullary. Most had an intermediate (66%) or poor (22%) International Metastatic Database Consortium risk. The best objective response included 6 partial responses (PRs; 33.3%) and 3 with stable disease (16.7%). Of the patients with a PR, the median time to the best response was 3.0 months, and median duration of the PR was 4.3 months. The median progression-free survival was 7.1 months. All-grade TRAEs were noted in 11 patients (61.1%) and included colitis (22%), hepatotoxicity (16%), rash (11%), and fatigue (11%). Eleven patients (61%) had TRAEs requiring high-dose glucocorticoids (> 40 mg of prednisone equivalent daily).
CONCLUSIONS
Ipilimumab plus nivolumab demonstrated objective responses and notable toxicity in patients with nccRCC.</snippet>
<snippet id="41176489">Title: Nationwide Real-World Outcomes of Trial Eligible and Trial Ineligible Patients With Metastatic Renal Cell Carcinoma Treated With Nivolumab Plus Ipilimumab.
Authors: Jespersen, Mette Syberg, Palshof, Jesper Andreas Evers, Fristrup, Niels et al. | Year: 2025 | Journal: Clinical genitourinary cancer
Abstract: INTRODUCTION
Clinical trials have demonstrated efficacy and safety of immune checkpoint inhibitor-based combination therapy in metastatic renal cell carcinoma (mRCC). However, patients who do not meet trial eligibility criteria constitute a large proportion of the real-world population, and their outcomes remain poorly described.
PATIENTS AND METHODS
This nationwide, retrospective cohort study included all Danish patients with mRCC who initiated nivolumab plus ipilimumab (NIVO/IPI) by May 5, 2022. Clinical data were obtained from electronic patient records. Outcomes included median progression-free survival (mPFS), median overall survival (mOS), and objective response rate (ORR), assessed by treating physicians. Patients were classified as trial-eligible or ineligible according to CheckMate 214 (CM214) key criteria. Survival was estimated using Kaplan-Meier methods, and subgroups were explored.
RESULTS
A total of 464 patients were included, with a median follow-up of 33 months. In the total cohort, mPFS was 9 months, mOS 41 months, and ORR 43%, including 13% complete responses. Among 282 trial-eligible patients, outcomes were comparable to CM214 with mPFS 12 months and mOS 49 month, while 182 ineligible patients had inferior outcomes, with mPFS 6 months and mOS 26 months (both P < .001). The presence of brain metastases did not adversely affect OS, while patients with autoimmune disease demonstrated unexpectedly favorable outcomes. Severe treatment-related toxicity (≥ grade 3) occurred in 44% in the total cohort, comparable to CM214.
CONCLUSION
This is the first nationwide real-world study evaluating NIVO/IPI outcomes in unselected mRCC. Trial-eligible patients achieved survival outcomes comparable to clinical trial results. Although ineligible patients derived less benefit, they still experienced meaningful clinical outcomes. These findings provide benchmark data for treatment of real-world mRCC populations in routine clinical practice.</snippet>

# Survival

- PD‑1 + CTLA‑4 (ipi/nivo): CheckMate 214 showed a statistically significant OS benefit over sunitinib in IMDC intermediate/poor‑risk mRCC, with median OS not reached in the double‑immune arm at ~28.2–NR versus 26.0 months for sunitinib. <cite id="29587324">CheckMate 214 demonstrated improved overall survival (Nivolumab plus Ipilimumab vs Sunitinib: median 28.2–NR vs 26.0 months; hazard ratio 0.63)</cite>. Real‑world cohorts corroborate this OS advantage, with median OS around 41–49 months for ipi/nivo versus ~26–28 months for sunitinib in trials, though outcomes vary by patient selection. <cite id="41176489">Trial‑eligible patients treated with nivolumab plus ipilimumab had median OS 49 months, close to CheckMate 214, while ineligible patients had shorter OS (26 months)</cite>.

- PD‑1 + VEGF‑TKI (e.g., nivo‑cabozantinib or nivo‑lenvatinib): Both CheckMate 284 (nivo‑cabozantinib) and CheckMate 9ER (nivo‑lenvatinib) demonstrated superior OS and PFS over sunitinib in first‑line mRCC. Network meta‑analysis indicates these regimens generally outperform double‑immune therapy in PFS and ORR, with nivolumab‑cabozantinib possibly offering the strongest OS benefit among immune combinations. <cite id="34546767">Regarding OS, nivolumab‑cabozantinib ranked first, followed by lenvatinib‑pembrolizumab, pembrolizumab‑axitinib, and nivolumab‑ipilimumab</cite>. <cite id="34546767">Regarding PFS and objective response rate, lenvatinib‑pembrolizumab ranked first, followed by nivolumab‑cabozantinib, pembrolizumab‑axitinib, and nivolumab‑ipilimumab</cite>.

# Toxicity

- PD‑1 + CTLA‑4 (ipi/nivo): Double‑checkpoint blockade has a higher rate of immune‑related adverse events and lower PFS compared with VEGF‑TKI combinations, but offers a favorable OS‑toxicity balance over sunitinib. <cite id="29587324">CheckMate 214 showed a considerable increase in immune-related adverse events with nivolumab‑ipilimumab compared with sunitinib, despite improved survival and quality of life</cite>. Real‑world cohorts report substantial grade ≥3 toxicity (≈40–44%) and characteristic toxicities such as colitis, hepatitis, rash, and endocrine disorders. <cite id="41176489">Severe treatment-related toxicity (≥ grade 3) occurred in 44% of patients treated with nivolumab plus ipilimumab in a nationwide real‑world cohort</cite>. <cite id="32800717">Common treatment‑related adverse events included colitis, hepatotoxicity, rash, and fatigue, with many requiring high‑dose corticosteroids</cite>.

- PD‑1 + VEGF‑TKI: These regimens generally achieve lower toxicity than double‑checkpoint blockade, with better PFS and OS versus sunitinib. Network meta‑analysis suggests nivolumab‑ipilimumab has the lowest grade 3+ toxicity among the compared regimens, while lenvatinib‑pembrolizumab and nivolumab‑cabozantinib prioritize PFS/ORR. <cite id="34546767">Nivolumab‑ipilimumab ranked first for lowest grade 3+ adverse events, followed by pembrolizumab‑axitinib, nivolumab‑cabozantinib, and lenvatinib‑pembrolizumab</cite>.

# Practical Interpretation

- For metastatic renal cell carcinoma, first‑line PD‑1/PD‑L1 plus VEGF‑TKI combinations (e.g., nivo‑cabozantinib, nivo‑lenvatinib, or pembrolizumab‑lenvatinib) provide strong PFS/ORR benefits and OS improvements over sunitinib with lower toxicity than CTLA‑4‑containing regimens, making them favorable options in broader risk groups. <cite id="34546767">Lenvatinib‑pembrolizumab showed the most favorable PFS and ORR, and nivolumab‑cabozantinib showed favorable OS</cite>.

- PD‑1 plus CTLA‑4 (nivo‑ipi) remains an effective option, particularly for intermediate/poor‑risk patients, with a clear OS advantage over sunitinib but higher immune‑related toxicity and lower PFS than VEGF‑TKI combinations. Careful patient selection and immune‑related adverse event monitoring are essential. <cite id="29587324">Nivolumab‑ipilimumab improved OS over sunitinib but increased immune-related adverse events</cite>. <cite id="41176489">Real‑world outcomes confirm meaningful survival benefit with substantial grade ≥3 toxicity in a sizable fraction of patients</cite>.

- Survival: PD‑1/PD‑L1 + VEGF‑TKI combinations (e.g., nivo‑cabozantinib, nivo‑lenvatinib, lenva‑t‑pembrolizumab) deliver robust PFS/ORR and OS gains over sunitinib, with nivolumab‑cabozantinib possibly offering the strongest OS signal among immune regimens. <cite id="34546767">Nivolumab‑cabozantinib ranked best for OS; lenvatinib‑pembrolizumab best for PFS and ORR</cite>. data.title: Clinical Outcomes and Adverse Events after First-Line Treatment in Metastatic Renal Cell Carcinoma: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis.
data.abstract:
PURPOSE
Four recent first-line clinical trials leveraging immune-oncology agents demonstrated an overall survival (OS) benefit relative to sunitinib. We aimed to provide formal comparisons among immune-oncology combinations in terms of OS, progression-free survival (PFS), objective response rates and treatment-related adverse events (AEs).
MATERIALS AND METHODS
PubMed® database was searched for studies indexed from January 1, 2016 through March 6, 2021. Only phase III randomized clinical trials with proven OS benefit relative to sunitinib were included: CheckMate 214 (nivolumab plus ipilimumab [N+I]), KEYNOTE-426 (pembrolizumab plus axitinib [P+A]), CheckMate 9ER (nivolumab plus cabozantinib [N+C]) and KEYNOTE-581 (lenvatinib plus permbrolizumab [L+P]). OS represented the primary outcome. PFS, objective response rate and AEs represented secondary outcomes.
RESULTS
Overall, 3,320 patients were included. Regarding OS, N+C ranked first, followed by L+P, P+A and N+I. Regarding PFS and objective response rate, L+P ranked first, followed by N+C, P+A and N+I. Finally, N+I ranked first with respect to lowest grade 3+ AEs, followed by P+A, N+C and L+P. Differences in followup duration, risk grouping and nephrectomy rates distinguish the studies.
CONCLUSIONS
N+C may provide the most favorable OS, L+P the most favorable PFS and ORRs, and N+I the lowest toxicity. Population differences may potentially undermine the generalizability and the robustness of findings of metastatic renal cell carcinoma.

Of the patients with a PR, the median time to the best response was 3.0 months, and median duration of the PR was 4.3 months. The median progression-free survival was 7.1 months. All-grade TRAEs were noted in 11 patients (61.1%) and included colitis (22%), hepatotoxicity (16%), rash (11%), and fatigue (11%). Eleven patients (61%) had TRAEs requiring high-dose glucocorticoids (> 40 mg of prednisone equivalent daily).
CONCLUSIONS
Ipilimumab plus nivolumab demonstrated objective responses and notable toxicity in patients with nccRCC.

data.title: Nationwide Real-World Outcomes of Trial Eligible and Trial Ineligible Patients With Metastatic Renal Cell Carcinoma Treated With Nivolumab Plus Ipilimumab.
data.abstract:
INTRODUCTION
Clinical trials have demonstrated efficacy and safety of immune checkpoint inhibitor-based combination therapy in metastatic renal cell carcinoma (mRCC). However, patients who do not meet trial eligibility criteria constitute a large proportion of the real-world population, and their outcomes remain poorly described.
PATIENTS AND METHODS
This nationwide, retrospective cohort study included all Danish patients with mRCC who initiated nivolumab plus ipilimumab (NIVO/IPI) by May 5, 2022. Clinical data were obtained from electronic patient records. Outcomes included median progression-free survival (mPFS), median overall survival (mOS), and objective response rate (ORR), assessed by treating physicians. Patients were classified as trial-eligible or ineligible according to CheckMate 214 (CM214) key criteria. Survival was estimated using Kaplan-Meier methods, and subgroups were explored.
RESULTS
A total of 464 patients were included, with a median follow-up of 33 months. In the total cohort, mPFS was 9 months, mOS 41 months, and ORR 43%, including 13% complete responses. Among 282 trial-eligible patients, outcomes were comparable to CM214 with mPFS 12 months and mOS 49 month, while 182 ineligible patients had inferior outcomes, with mPFS 6 months and mOS 26 months (both P < .001). The presence of brain metastases did not adversely affect OS, while patients with autoimmune disease demonstrated unexpectedly favorable outcomes. Severe treatment-related toxicity (≥ grade 3) occurred in 44% in the total cohort, comparable to CM214.
CONCLUSION
This is the first nationwide real-world study evaluating NIVO/IPI outcomes in unselected mRCC. Trial-eligible patients achieved survival outcomes comparable to clinical trial results. Although ineligible patients derived less benefit, they still experienced meaningful clinical outcomes. These findings provide benchmark data for treatment of real-world mRCC populations in routine clinical practice.

# Summary

- First-line PD‑1/PD‑L1 plus CTLA‑4 (ipi/nivo) improves overall survival (OS) versus sunitinib in intermediate/poor‑risk metastatic renal cell carcinoma (mRCC), but with higher immune‑related toxicity. In CheckMate 214, the doublet achieved a median OS that was not reached at 28.2–NR versus 26.0 months with sunitinib and had a favorable OS‑toxicity trade‑off compared with sunitinib, albeit with increased immune adverse events and lower PFS compared with single‑agent PD‑1 or with VEGF‑TKI combinations. <cite id="29587324">CheckMate 214, a randomized phase-3 trial, demonstrated improved overall survival (Nivolumab plus Ipilimumab vs Sunitinib: median 28.2–NR vs 26.0 months; hazard ratio 0.63) and better side effect profile and quality of life compared with Sunitinib, but with a considerable increase in immune-related adverse events</cite>. <cite id="32800717">Ipilimumab plus nivolumab demonstrated objective responses and notable toxicity in patients with non-clear cell RCC, reflecting the immune-related adverse event profile characteristic of CTLA‑4‑targeted regimens</cite>. <cite id="41176489">Real‑world cohorts treated with nivolumab plus ipilimumab show median PFS ~9–12 months and median OS ~41–49 months, with ~44% experiencing severe (grade ≥3) treatment‑related toxicity, consistent with trial‑expected toxicity</cite>.

- First-line PD‑1/PD‑L1 plus VEGF‑TKI (e.g., nivo‑cabozantinib [CheckMate 284] or nivo‑lenva‑t inib [CheckMate 9ER]) improves PFS and OS versus sunitinib and has lower toxicity than double‑checkpoint blockade. Network meta‑analysis comparing four immune first‑line regimens suggests lenvatinib‑pembrolizumab may offer the most favorable PFS and objective response rate, nivolumab‑cabozantinib may favor OS, and nivolumab‑ipilimumab has the lowest grade 3+ toxicity among these regimens. <cite id="34546767">A 2022 systematic review and network meta‑analysis of first‑line immune combinations in mRCC found: nivolumab‑cabozantinib ranked best for OS, lenvatinib‑pembrolizumab ranked best for PFS and objective response rate, and nivolumab‑ipilimumab had the lowest grade 3+ adverse events</cite>.

# Survival

- PD‑1 + CTLA‑4 (ipi/nivo): CheckMate 214 showed a statistically significant OS benefit over sunitinib in IMDC intermediate/poor‑risk mRCC, with median OS not reached in the double‑immune arm at ~28.2–NR versus 26.0 months for sunitinib. <cite id="29587324">CheckMate 214 demonstrated improved overall survival (Nivolumab plus Ipilimumab vs Sunitinib: median 28.2–NR vs 26.0 months; hazard ratio 0.63)</cite>. Real‑world cohorts corroborate this OS advantage, with median OS around 41–49 months for ipi/nivo versus ~26–28 months for sunitinib in trials, though outcomes vary by patient selection. <cite id="41176489">Trial‑eligible patients treated with nivolumab plus ipilimumab had median OS 49 months, close to CheckMate 214, while ineligible patients had shorter OS (26 months)</cite>.

- PD‑1 + VEGF‑TKI (e.g., nivo‑cabozantinib or nivo‑lenvatinib): Both CheckMate 284 (nivo‑cabozantinib) and CheckMate 9ER (nivo‑lenvatinib) demonstrated superior OS and PFS over sunitinib in first‑line mRCC. Network meta‑analysis indicates these regimens generally outperform double‑immune therapy in PFS and ORR, with nivolumab‑cabozantinib possibly offering the strongest OS benefit among immune combinations. <cite id="34546767">Regarding OS, nivolumab‑cabozantinib ranked first, followed by lenvatinib‑pembrolizumab, pembrolizumab‑axitinib, and nivolumab‑ipilimumab</cite>. <cite id="34546767">Regarding PFS and objective response rate, lenvatinib‑pembrolizumab ranked first, followed by nivolumab‑cabozantinib, pembrolizumab‑axitinib, and nivolumab‑ipilimumab</cite>.

# Toxicity

- PD‑1 + CTLA‑4 (ipi/nivo): Double‑checkpoint blockade has a higher rate of immune‑related adverse events and lower PFS compared with VEGF‑TKI combinations, but offers a favorable OS‑toxicity balance over sunitinib. <cite id="29587324">CheckMate 214 showed a considerable increase in immune-related adverse events with nivolumab‑ipilimumab compared with sunitinib, despite improved survival and quality of life</cite>. Real‑world cohorts report substantial grade ≥3 toxicity (≈40–44%) and characteristic toxicities such as colitis, hepatitis, rash, and endocrine disorders. <cite id="41176489">Severe treatment-related toxicity (≥ grade 3) occurred in 44% of patients treated with nivolumab plus ipilimumab in a nationwide real‑world cohort</cite>. <cite id="32800717">Common treatment‑related adverse events included colitis, hepatotoxicity, rash, and fatigue, with many requiring high‑dose corticosteroids</cite>.

- PD‑1 + VEGF‑TKI: These regimens generally achieve lower toxicity than double‑checkpoint blockade, with better PFS and OS versus sunitinib. Network meta‑analysis suggests nivolumab‑ipilimumab has the lowest grade 3+ toxicity among the compared regimens, while lenvatinib‑pembrolizumab and nivolumab‑cabozantinib prioritize PFS/ORR. <cite id="34546767">Nivolumab‑ipilimumab ranked first for lowest grade 3+ adverse events, followed by pembrolizumab‑axitinib, nivolumab‑cabozantinib, and lenvatinib‑pembrolizumab</cite>.

# Practical Interpretation

- For metastatic renal cell carcinoma, first‑line PD‑1/PD‑L1 plus VEGF‑TKI combinations (e.g., nivo‑cabozantinib, nivo‑lenvatinib, or pembrolizumab‑lenvatinib) provide strong PFS/ORR benefits and OS improvements over sunitinib with lower toxicity than CTLA‑4‑containing regimens, making them favorable options in broader risk groups. <cite id="34546767">Lenvatinib‑pembrolizumab showed the most favorable PFS and ORR, and nivolumab‑cabozantinib showed favorable OS</cite>.

- PD‑1 plus CTLA‑4 (nivo‑ipi) remains an effective option, particularly for intermediate/poor‑risk patients, with a clear OS advantage over sunitinib but higher immune‑related toxicity and lower PFS than VEGF‑TKI combinations. Careful patient selection and immune‑related adverse event monitoring are essential. <cite id="29587324">Nivolumab‑ipilimumab improved OS over sunitinib but increased immune-related adverse events</cite>. <cite id="41176489">Real‑world outcomes confirm meaningful survival benefit with substantial grade ≥3 toxicity in a sizable fraction of patients</cite>.

- Population differences (e.g., age, performance status, comorbidities) can influence observed survival and toxicity across regimens, and subgroup analyses may show heterogeneity in benefit. <cite id="34546767">Differences in follow-up duration, risk grouping, and nephrectomy rates may affect generalizability of comparative findings across trials</cite>. <cite id="39941888">In elderly or poor performance status patients, outcomes with ipi/nivo can mirror trial‑based toxicity and survival patterns, with worse OS and PFS in those with poor KPS</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- Survival: PD‑1/PD‑L1 + VEGF‑TKI combinations (e.g., nivo‑cabozantinib, nivo‑lenvatinib, lenva‑t‑pembrolizumab) deliver robust PFS/ORR and OS gains over sunitinib, with nivolumab‑cabozantinib possibly offering the strongest OS signal among immune regimens. <cite id="34546767">Nivolumab‑cabozantinib ranked best for OS; lenvatinib‑pembrolizumab best for PFS and ORR</cite>. PD‑1 + CTLA‑4 (nivo‑ipi) also improves OS over sunitinib, with CheckMate 214 demonstrating a median OS advantage not reached in the double‑immune arm versus 26 months with sunitinib. <cite id="29587324">Nivolumab plus Ipilimumab improved OS over sunitinib (median 28.2–NR vs 26.0 months)</cite>.

- Toxicity: PD‑1 + CTLA‑4 regimens have higher immune‑related toxicity (≈40–44% grade ≥3) and lower PFS than VEGF‑TKI combinations, whereas PD‑1 + VEGF‑TKIs generally offer a more favorable toxicity profile and better PFS/ORR than double‑checkpoint blockade. <cite id="29587324">Double‑checkpoint therapy increased immune-related adverse events compared with sunitinib</cite>. <cite id="41176489">Severe toxicity (grade ≥3) occurred in 44% in real‑world nivo‑ipi practice</cite>. <cite id="34546767">Nivolumab‑ipilimumab had the lowest grade 3+ toxicity among compared regimens, while lenvatinib‑pembrolizumab led in PFS/ORR</cite>.

Overall, for first‑line metastatic RCC, PD‑1/PD‑L1 plus VEGF‑TKI therapy generally yields superior PFS and often better OS than sunitinib with lower toxicity than PD‑1 plus CTLA‑4, while PD‑1 plus CTLA‑4 remains a high‑efficacy option with a more toxic profile that may be preferred in selected intermediate/poor‑risk patients. <cite id="34546767">Across immune combinations, lenvatinib‑pembrolizumab favors PFS/ORR, nivolumab‑cabozantinib favors OS, and nivolumab‑ipilimumab has the lowest grade 3+ toxicity</cite>. <cite id="29587324">Nivolumab‑ipilimumab improves OS over sunitinib but increases immune-related adverse events</cite>. <cite id="41176489">Real‑world nivolumab‑ipilimumab cohorts confirm meaningful survival benefit alongside substantial grade ≥3 toxicity</cite>.

<snippet id="22231479">Title: Efficacy and safety of rituximab in patients with active proliferative lupus nephritis: the Lupus Nephritis Assessment with Rituximab study.
Authors: Rovin, Brad H, Furie, Richard, Latinis, Kevin et al. | Year: 2012 | Journal: Arthritis and rheumatism
Abstract: OBJECTIVE
To evaluate the efficacy and safety of rituximab in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase III trial in patients with lupus nephritis treated concomitantly with mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) and corticosteroids.
METHODS
Patients (n = 144) with class III or class IV lupus nephritis were randomized 1:1 to receive rituximab (1,000 mg) or placebo on days 1, 15, 168, and 182. The primary end point was renal response status at week 52.
RESULTS
Rituximab depleted peripheral CD19+ B cells in 71 of 72 patients. The overall (complete and partial) renal response rates were 45.8% among the 72 patients receiving placebo and 56.9% among the 72 patients receiving rituximab (P = 0.18); partial responses accounted for most of the difference. The primary end point (superior response rate with rituximab) was not achieved. Eight placebo-treated patients and no rituximab-treated patients required cyclophosphamide rescue therapy through week 52. Statistically significant improvements in serum complement C3, C4, and anti-double-stranded DNA (anti-dsDNA) levels were observed among patients treated with rituximab. In both treatment groups, a reduction in anti-dsDNA levels greater than the median reduction was associated with reduced proteinuria. The rates of serious adverse events, including infections, were similar in both groups. Neutropenia, leukopenia, and hypotension occurred more frequently in the rituximab group.
CONCLUSION
Although rituximab therapy led to more responders and greater reductions in anti-dsDNA and C3/C4 levels, it did not improve clinical outcomes after 1 year of treatment. The combination of rituximab with MMF and corticosteroids did not result in any new or unexpected safety signals.</snippet>
<snippet id="29410944">Title: Clinical Outcomes Observed among Biopsy Proven Lupus Nephritis Patients Treated with Mycophenolate Mofetil as First-line Therapy.
Authors: Timlin, Homa, Magder, Laurence, Petri, Michelle | Year: 2017 | Journal: Cureus
Abstract: Background and objective The rate of end-stage renal disease from lupus nephritis has not declined, in spite of recent advances in therapeutics, such as mycophenolate mofetil (MMF). To provide insight into rates of the clinical outcomes in current practice after biopsy-proven lupus nephritis, we used a prospective cohort of the patients with newly diagnosed lupus nephritis, treated with MMF and observed their outcomes. Method Twenty systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) patients who began mycophenolate mofetil shortly after a biopsy-confirmed diagnosis of lupus nephritis were included in the analysis. There were five patients with class III, nine with class IV, four with class III-V, one with class IV-V and two with class V lupus nephritis. The initial dose of mycophenolate mofetil was 1000 mg twice daily. If no improvement was observed, the dose was increased to 1500 mg twice daily after one month. We estimated the survival function for the time until the urine protein/creatinine reached 0.50 grams or less, after starting MMF by using an approach that accommodated interval-censored data. We also evaluated the treatment response using five different sets of criteria for the response that have previously been used in the clinical trials. These included the Bristol Myers-Squibb (BMS), the American College of Rheumatology (ACR), the lupus nephritis assessment with rituximab (LUNAR ), the Aspreva Lupus Management Study (ALMS), and the Abatacept and Cyclophosphamide Combination Efficacy and Safety Study (ACCESS). Result We estimated that 52% of the SLE patients reached 0.50 grams of proteinuria within 51 days of starting mycophenolate mofetil (95% confidence interval 29%-74%) and 77% reached 0.50 grams or less within 260 days (95% confidence interval 57%-97%). The probability of response at 90 and 180 days was 5% and 33% (the Bristol Myers-Squibb), 26% and 57% (the American College of Rheumatology), and 11% and 28% (the lupus nephritis assessment with rituximab, the Aspreva Lupus Management Study and the Abatacept and Cyclophosphamide Combination Efficacy and Safety Study). Conclusion The complete renal response ranged from 28% to 57% at six months in the routine clinical practice, mirroring the results in randomized clinical trials. Regardless of the response measures, the complete renal response was slow and, by most indices, reached in only a minority of the patients by the end of six months of the induction therapy. This indicates the urgent need for the faster and more effective lupus nephritis treatments.</snippet>

<snippet id="19369404">Title: Mycophenolate mofetil versus cyclophosphamide for induction treatment of lupus nephritis.
Authors: Appel, Gerald B, Contreras, Gabriel, Dooley, Mary Anne et al. | Year: 2009 | Journal: Journal of the American Society of Nephrology : JASN
Abstract: Recent studies have suggested that mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) may offer advantages over intravenous cyclophosphamide (IVC) for the treatment of lupus nephritis, but these therapies have not been compared in an international randomized, controlled trial. Here, we report the comparison of MMF and IVC as induction treatment for active lupus nephritis in a multinational, two-phase (induction and maintenance) study. We randomly assigned 370 patients with classes III through V lupus nephritis to open-label MMF (target dosage 3 g/d) or IVC (0.5 to 1.0 g/m(2) in monthly pulses) in a 24-wk induction study. Both groups received prednisone, tapered from a maximum starting dosage of 60 mg/d. The primary end point was a prespecified decrease in urine protein/creatinine ratio and stabilization or improvement in serum creatinine. Secondary end points included complete renal remission, systemic disease activity and damage, and safety. Overall, we did not detect a significantly different response rate between the two groups: 104 (56.2%) of 185 patients responded to MMF compared with 98 (53.0%) of 185 to IVC. Secondary end points were also similar between treatment groups. There were nine deaths in the MMF group and five in the IVC group. We did not detect significant differences between the MMF and IVC groups with regard to rates of adverse events, serious adverse events, or infections. Although most patients in both treatment groups experienced clinical improvement, the study did not meet its primary objective of showing that MMF was superior to IVC as induction treatment for lupus nephritis.</snippet>
<snippet id="25383558">Title: Multitarget therapy for induction treatment of lupus nephritis: a randomized trial.
Authors: Liu, Zhihong, Zhang, Haitao, Liu, Zhangsuo et al. | Year: 2015 | Journal: Annals of internal medicine
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Treatment of lupus nephritis (LN) remains challenging.
OBJECTIVE
To assess the efficacy and safety of a multitarget therapy consisting of tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and steroid compared with intravenous cyclophosphamide and steroid as induction therapy for LN.
DESIGN
24-week randomized, open-label, multicenter study. (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT00876616).
SETTING
26 renal centers in China.
PATIENTS
Adults (aged 18 to 65 years) with biopsy-proven LN.
INTERVENTION
Tacrolimus, 4 mg/d, and mycophenolate mofetil, 1.0 g/d, versus intravenous cyclophosphamide with a starting dose of 0.75 (adjusted to 0.5 to 1.0) g/m2 of body surface area every 4 weeks for 6 months. Both groups received 3 days of pulse methylprednisolone followed by a tapering course of oral prednisone therapy.
MEASUREMENTS
The primary end point was complete remission at 24 weeks. Secondary end points included overall response (complete and partial remission), time to overall response, and adverse events.
RESULTS
After 24 weeks of therapy, more patients in the multitarget group (45.9%) than in the intravenous cyclophosphamide group (25.6%) showed complete remission (difference, 20.3 percentage points [95% CI, 10.0 to 30.6 percentage points]; P < 0.001). The overall response incidence was higher in the multitarget group than in the intravenous cyclophosphamide group (83.5% vs. 63.0%; difference, 20.4 percentage points [CI, 10.3 to 30.6 percentage points]; P < 0.001), and the median time to overall response was shorter in the multitarget group (difference, -4.1 weeks [CI, -7.9 to -2.1 weeks]). Incidence of adverse events did not differ between the multitarget and intravenous cyclophosphamide groups (50.3% [91 of 181] vs. 52.5% [95 of 181]).
LIMITATION
The study was limited to 24 weeks of follow-up.
CONCLUSION
Multitarget therapy provides superior efficacy compared with intravenous cyclophosphamide as induction therapy for LN.
PRIMARY FUNDING SOURCE
National Basic Research Program of China, National Key Technology R&D Program.</snippet>
<snippet id="32486934">Title: Rituximab use as induction therapy for lupus nephritis: a systematic review.
Authors: Stolyar, Liya, Lahita, Robert G, Panush, Richard S | Year: 2020 | Journal: Lupus
Abstract: OBJECTIVE
Rituximab (RTX) has important usage in rheumatoid arthritis and vasculitis. There remains a need for more, better, and safer treatments for patients with lupus nephritis (LN). RTX has been trialed in such patients without definitive conclusions about its effectiveness. As a role for RTX has not been clearly established for LN, we carried out a systematic review and analysis.
METHODS
We identified 31 studies of RTX for class I-VI LN, and assessed complete renal response (CRR) and partial renal response (PRR) using criteria including serum creatinine, proteinuria, and urinary sediment. Due to differences in the pediatric presentation of the disease, studies focusing on pediatric patients were excluded.
RESULTS
One randomized controlled trial (RCT) showed superiority of RTX+cyclophosphamide (CYC) versus CYC alone (64% vs. 21% CRR and 19% vs. 36% PRR). Six prospective and retrospective studies utilizing RTX monotherapy found 66% CRR or PRR in all patients. Eleven studies that investigated RTX in combination with CYC or mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) also found 66% CRR or PRR in all patients. In total, the CRR for Caucasian, East Asian, and Hispanic patients were 77%, 38%, and 28%, respectively.
CONCLUSIONS
